strengths: Proposes a parameter-free KV cache compression method using DCT low-pass filtering, motivated by a power-spectrum analysis of LLaMA-2 KV states; applicable to both fine-tuning and inference without architectural changes.
Introduces an iterative compression mechanism that limits attention cache size and compresses keys before RoPE, avoiding out-of-bound position embeddings and enabling context extension.
Reports competitive perplexity on PG-19 and Proof-pile with LLaMA-2, including extrapolation from 8K training to 64K evaluation, and positive LongBench/Needle-in-a-Haystack results.
Provides efficiency analysis showing negligible DCT/IDCT overhead in latency and FLOPs, with decoding time growing approximately linearly rather than quadratically.
Includes some useful appendices: head-wise power spectrum analysis, RoPE-compression ablation, training settings, and compression overhead measurements.
The core idea of frequency-domain KV compression for decoder-only LLMs is reasonably novel and could be practically useful if evaluated more rigorously.
weaknesses: Major evaluation fairness issue: on LongBench and Needle-in-a-Haystack, FreqKV is fine-tuned with LoRA/SFT on LongAlpaca, while several baselines (SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite, LongHeads) are training-free inference-time compression or zero-shot methods. There is no comparison against LongLoRA, LoCoCo, Activation Beacon, or full-attention SFT under the same fine-tuning protocol, so the claimed SOTA downstream understanding is not supported.

Limited novelty: DCT-based low-pass filtering is a standard signal-processing operation. The paper does not compare against simple time-domain downsampling/pooling, learned projections, PCA, random projection, or FFT/other frequency transforms. Thus it is unclear whether the gains come specifically from frequency-domain processing rather than any aggressive KV bottleneck plus fine-tuning.

The empirical motivation is weak: power-spectrum concentration is averaged over many documents and hidden dimensions and does not guarantee per-instance/per-token/per-layer concentration. Layer 0 shows no obvious concentration, yet all layers are compressed; there is no layer-wise or head-wise adaptive compression strategy.

Theoretical support is missing: no error bounds or formal justification for discarding high-frequency components, and no analysis of iterative re-compression of already compressed linear combinations. Energy concentration does not necessarily imply information redundancy, especially for retrieval or local-detail tasks.

Ablations are incomplete: only retaining ratio and compression-before/after-RoPE are studied. Missing ablations include DCT vs. FFT vs. time-domain downsampling, compression interval, sink token count, chunk size, layer-wise ratios, and training-free vs. fine-tuned variants. Dropping is compared only on Needle-in-a-Haystack, not on perplexity or LongBench.

The LongBench table compares against inference-time compression baselines without controlling for the strong effect of LongAlpaca SFT. Improvements may be due to supervised fine-tuning rather than FreqKV. Aggregate scores and statistical significance are also not reported.

Position/RoPE handling is not fully specified: compressed tokens are assigned cache positions, but it is unclear how incoming uncompressed tokens and queries are positioned after iterative compression. Mixing cache-relative and original positions may introduce hidden inconsistencies that are only partially addressed by fine-tuning.

Some claims are overstated or imprecise: the abstract says the cache is compressed to a fixed size, but the cache size actually oscillates between the retaining size and the original window; the method requires fine-tuning, so 'efficient context extension' is not zero-shot.

Reproducibility is limited: exact LongBench prompt formats, data preprocessing, baseline fine-tuning details, and code availability are not clearly provided. Baseline reproductions may not follow official settings identically, making comparisons uncertain.

strengths: Introduces a novel application of frequency-domain compression to KV cache for decoder-only LLMs, with the observation that KV energy concentrates in low-frequency components across layers.
The method is simple, introduces no additional parameters or architectural modules, and can be combined with existing LLMs and FlashAttention-style implementations.
Iterative compression bounds the KV cache size during decoding and enables context extension with minimal fine-tuning, showing promising perplexity and Needle-in-a-Haystack results.
Provides useful analyses of retaining ratio, decoding latency, and FLOPs overhead, and demonstrates context extension up to 64K tokens in some settings.
weaknesses: LongBench comparisons are not fair: FreqKV is fine-tuned on LongAlpaca, while baselines such as SnapKV, PyramidKV, LM-Infinite, and LongHeads are training-free or evaluated under different settings. A control with long-context SFT using full attention is missing, so gains may come from SFT rather than frequency-domain compression.

Important baselines and ablations are missing, including Activation Beacon, LongLoRA with full cache on LongBench, and simple time-domain compression/downsampling or pooling. Without these, it is unclear whether the frequency-domain operation is necessary or superior to simpler alternatives.

The technical motivation is weak: average power-spectrum concentration does not prove that high-frequency KV components are redundant for attention, since attention depends on query-key interactions and low-energy components can still be important. Layer-wise behavior is ignored; layer 0 lacks concentration yet compression appears uniformly applied, with no per-layer ablation.

Position-embedding handling is unclear and potentially problematic: keys are compressed before RoPE and re-indexed within the cache, which changes relative positions. The paper does not sufficiently explain or ablate this design, and it may limit the method's generality.

Evaluation consistency and rigor are limited: PPL comparisons rely on LongLoRA numbers reported in another paper rather than reproduced under the same training setup; LongBench baselines come from mixed sources. Memory usage, a main claimed benefit, is not measured. Claims of SOTA are therefore overstated.

Novelty is incremental: low-pass filtering of KV states via DCT is straightforward, with no theoretical guarantee or analysis of iterative information loss and error accumulation across compression rounds. The method is heuristic.

Reproducibility and clarity are insufficient: key implementation details (chunk-wise training with compression, PPL computation with compressed cache, loss backpropagation through DCT/IDCT, sink-token choice, hyperparameter selection) are missing or vague. No code release is mentioned, and tables have formatting/column-name issues.

Results are mixed: FreqKV is not consistently better than LongLoRA or full-cache baselines, especially on Proof-pile and several LongBench tasks, so the central claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Introduces a novel and simple frequency-domain KV cache compression method for decoder-only LLMs, motivated by an empirical analysis showing low-frequency energy concentration in KV states across layers.

Requires no additional parameters or architectural changes, and the iterative compression scheme bounds attention cache size while avoiding position extrapolation/interpolation in the way it handles RoPE key states.

Provides a reasonably broad empirical evaluation: long-context language modeling on PG-19 and Proof-pile, long-context understanding on LongBench, and Needle-in-a-Haystack, plus analyses of retaining ratio, decoding latency, FLOPs, and head-wise power spectra.

Achieves competitive or improved results against strong baselines such as LongLoRA, LoCoCo, SnapKV, PyramidKV, and Dropping in several settings, especially on long-context understanding tasks and Needle-in-a-Haystack.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with useful practical analyses showing that the compression overhead is small relative to decoding time and FLOPs.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness is a concern: LongBench compares a fine-tuned FreqKV model with mostly training-free or differently tuned KV compression baselines, so the reported gains may partly reflect additional supervised fine-tuning rather than the frequency-domain compression itself.

Ablations are limited. The paper mainly studies retaining ratio and fixes sink size to 4; it does not ablate sink size, compression interval, layer-specific retaining ratios, alternative frequency transforms, or simple downsampling/merging under the same fine-tuning protocol.

Theoretical justification is thin. The energy-concentration observation is empirical, and low-pass DCT along the sequence dimension globally mixes tokens, which could remove high-frequency information needed for precise retrieval; there is no formal guarantee or analysis of iterative compression error accumulation.

The PPL results are surprisingly insensitive to training length: models trained at 8K, 16K, and 32K yield nearly identical PG-19 and Proof-pile perplexities. This is not fully explained and deserves more investigation.

Position handling and chunk-wise attention details are somewhat underspecified. It is not fully clear how position indices are assigned to compressed cache entries and incoming tokens, how this affects long-range order, and whether all baselines follow the same positional treatment.

Reproducibility could be improved: no code release is mentioned, some tables/figures are poorly formatted in the submitted version, and the exact fine-tuning/alignment protocol is not always sufficient to fully reproduce the comparison baselines.

Some LongBench results are inconsistent, with FreqKV underperforming baselines on tasks such as Mf-en, TKLC, and summarization subtasks, and no statistical significance or variance is reported for the main benchmark comparisons.

strengths: Introduces a novel and simple frequency-domain KV cache compression method for decoder-only LLMs, with no additional architectural parameters.

Broad empirical evaluation across LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, LongGenBench, PG-19, and Proof-pile, including ablations on retaining ratio, sink size, high/low frequency, RoPE placement, and rescaling.

Demonstrates practical efficiency benefits: low compression overhead, approximately linear decoding time, reduced training time/memory, and stable perplexity when extrapolating to very long PG-19 contexts.
Clear motivation grounded in power spectrum analysis and perturbation/summarization experiments showing low-frequency KV components carry more global information.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness is questionable: FreqKV is fine-tuned on LongAlpaca/RedPajama for the main benchmarks while many eviction/merging baselines are training-free or not similarly fine-tuned, so performance gains may stem from supervised fine-tuning rather than the compression method itself.

The reported retaining ratio is misleading for cache-size comparisons. FreqKV compresses only when the cache reaches N, then lets it grow back to N, so the average cache size is roughly (L+N)/2. At gamma=1%, the effective average cache is near 50%, making comparisons against constant 1% baselines invalid and undermining the claimed robustness at 1% retention.

The claim of extending context to 256K is supported only by language-modeling perplexity on PG-19. There is no long-context understanding or generation evaluation at such lengths, and even at 16K RULER performance degrades substantially (e.g., average 47.3, NIAH 25.47), which conflicts with the stated robustness.

The technical justification for truncating DCT coefficients and applying an L-point IDCT is not rigorous; the rescaling factor is heuristic and may not correspond to a principled low-pass reconstruction of the original sequence.

Baseline results and comparisons are inconsistent or incomplete in places, e.g., in RULER some methods match the full-cache LLaMA-3 exactly at 8K, and LongBench has many missing baseline entries, making the claimed SOTA comparisons less reliable.

Overclaims are present: the method is called parameter-free yet requires fine-tuning, is called architecture-agnostic although only LLaMA models are tested, and the code URL is left incomplete in the manuscript.
Needle-in-a-Haystack results are shown only as figures without numerical values, and the strong qualitative claim is not sufficiently supported by quantitative evidence.

strengths: Proposes a novel frequency-domain KV compression approach for decoder-only LLMs, using DCT low-pass filtering and iterative compression. The idea is simple, parameter-free at the compression-module level, and architecture-agnostic.
Includes a RoPE-before-compression design that avoids out-of-bound position embeddings and allows iterative cache compression without position interpolation/extrapolation.

Extensive empirical evaluation on language modeling, LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, with many baselines and ablations on retaining ratio, sink size, frequency selection, rescaling, and overhead.
Provides efficiency analyses showing reduced training memory/time, negligible compression FLOPs/latency, and stable PPL extrapolation up to 256K on PG-19.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: code is provided, implementation details are mostly clear, and multiple appendices give additional settings and analyses.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are unfair: FreqKV is fine-tuned/SFT for context extension, while many KV-compression baselines are training-free and evaluated beyond the model's native window. In LongBench, RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongGenBench, there is no fine-tuned full-cache or full-attention context-extension baseline, so reported gains may come from fine-tuning rather than frequency-domain compression.

The abstract's 'parameter-free' claim is misleading: although the compression operation adds no parameters, the method relies on LoRA fine-tuning and learnable embedding/normalization layers, i.e., it requires training to work well.

The claim that FreqKV 'preserves the information of all tokens' is false: discarding high-frequency components explicitly loses information, and the method may harm exact retrieval and local-detail tasks. RULER at 16K shows NIAH 25.47, CWE 45.10, and VT 44.60, which are far from robust extension despite the paper's emphasis.

The RULER and Needle-in-a-Haystack comparisons are especially problematic: baselines collapse at 16K largely because they use out-of-bound position embeddings without context extension, rather than because FreqKV's compression is inherently superior. A fair comparison would fine-tune/adapt baselines to the extended context as well.

Theoretical justification is thin. DCT low-pass filtering along the sequence dimension assumes smoothness and global information concentration, but the paper provides no error bounds or formal analysis of iterative compression, positional reindexing of compressed pseudo-tokens, or per-head/per-layer variability.

LongBench results contain missing entries and inconsistent comparison settings, and some average gains are small (e.g., LLaMA-3-instruct: FreqKV 43.48 vs full cache 42.51). Without a fine-tuned full-cache reference under the same SFT recipe, the claimed superiority is not established.

Ablations focus mostly on perplexity. There is little downstream ablation on the effect of retaining ratio, sink size, and frequency-band choice, so the practical robustness of these hyperparameters on understanding/generation tasks remains unclear.

Overall, the central claims are stronger than the evidence: the method extends context, but absolute performance at 16K on retrieval-heavy RULER tasks is weak, and the paper does not sufficiently separate the effects of compression from those of fine-tuning and context extension.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated: first work to apply frequency-domain compression to KV cache for decoder-only LLMs, with a clear empirical observation that KV states concentrate energy in low-frequency components.
Parameter-free and architecture-agnostic: introduces no additional parameters or architectural modifications, and can be integrated into existing models via iterative compression.
Strong empirical results: consistently outperforms eviction- and merging-based baselines on LongBench, RULER, and LongGenBench, and extends LLaMA-2-7B to 256K context with stable perplexity.

Comprehensive evaluation and analysis: covers multiple model sizes, prefilling and decoding scenarios, extensive baselines, ablations (retaining ratio, sink size, RoPE integration, rescaling), and efficiency/overhead measurements.
Reproducibility: code is provided, training details are summarized, and the paper includes ethics and reproducibility statements.
Practical efficiency: demonstrates reduced training time/memory and negligible compression overhead, making the method attractive for long-context inference.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is a concern: FreqKV is fine-tuned with its compression pattern, while several inference-time baselines (e.g., SnapKV, PyramidKV) are training-free or not equivalently adapted, which may advantage FreqKV.

Absolute performance at extended contexts remains limited: on RULER 16K, FreqKV averages only 47.30 with NIAH 25.47, far below its 8K performance, so the claim of robust context extension needs qualification for retrieval-heavy tasks.

The low-frequency dominance assumption is mostly shown via averaged spectra and may not hold universally across layers, heads, or data types (e.g., formula-heavy Proof-pile), where high-frequency/local details matter.
Limited comparison with other context-extension paradigms such as positional interpolation, NTK, or YaRN, which could be stronger or complementary baselines for long-context extension.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: retaining ratio, sink size, chunk size, and training length affect performance, and optimal settings may be task-dependent despite the provided ablations.
The term 'parameter-free' is slightly misleading: the method requires fine-tuning and several hyperparameters, even though it adds no new model parameters.
